stories.title: EvilTokens: a phishing-as-a-service kit that steals Microsoft 365 tokens through device code phishing
stories.summary: EvilTokens is a phishing-as-a-service platform that appeared in February 2026 and abuses the OAuth device code flow. Microsoft says its campaigns compromised more than 12,000 inboxes in over 10,000 organizations. The victim is shown a real device code and sent to the genuine microsoft.com/devicelogin page, so the sign-in and MFA are done by the victim and the attacker receives the tokens without ever seeing a password. Stolen tokens were used to read and exfiltrate mail, create inbox rules and in some cases register a device to obtain a Primary Refresh Token. Microsoft's Digital Crimes Unit coordinated a disruption of the infrastructure.

timeline.text: EvilTokens emerges as a phishing-as-a-service platform sold through Telegram. (Microsoft gives the month only; the 1st is a placeholder.)
Microsoft tracks a related campaign that used automation platforms to start short-lived polling nodes running Node.js backend logic. (Microsoft gives the month only; the 1st is a placeholder.)
Microsoft Threat Intelligence publishes its analysis and describes the coordinated disruption by the Digital Crimes Unit.

stories.rootCause: The device code flow lets a third party start a sign-in that the victim completes on a legitimate Microsoft page. Where Conditional Access does not block the flow, the attacker's polling script receives valid tokens after the victim signs in with MFA.
attacker: Developer and operator of the kit is tracked as Storm-2992; sold on Telegram for $1,500 plus $500 per month.

Lures by email (invoices, RFPs, shared files, password-expiry notices) with URLs, PDF or HTML attachments, behind fake CAPTCHA pages and multi-stage redirects on Vercel, Cloudflare Workers and AWS Lambda.
A background script requests a live device code, shows it with Copy Code and Continue buttons and polls the actor's /state endpoint every three to five seconds for up to 15 minutes.

After sign-in: Microsoft Graph reconnaissance, AI-assisted search for financial and executive mailboxes, wire-transfer and invoice keywords, malicious inbox rules, and device registration to obtain a Primary Refresh Token within about 10 minutes.
iocs: Hosting abused: .vercel.app, .workers.dev, AWS Lambda (named by Microsoft)
Microsoft lists no IP addresses or file hashes in this post

remediation.text: Block the device code flow with Conditional Access wherever possible; where Teams devices need it, scope the exception to the Teams device resource accounts and exclude the Device Registration Service resource.
Revoke refresh tokens with revokeSignInSessions for a suspected account and consider disabling it temporarily; access tokens can stay valid for up to an hour.
Require phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO, Authenticator with passkeys), enable sign-in risk policies and Continuous Access Evaluation, block legacy authentication.
Configure anti-phishing, Safe Links and ZAP, raise the Advanced Phishing Threshold to 2 or 3 and alert on suspicious inbox rule creation.

stories.title: Storm-3168 (JADEPUFFER): agentic destructive attack in Azure through compromised service principals
stories.summary: Microsoft investigated malicious Azure activity in one compromised tenant where two service principals were used: one for reconnaissance, the other for discovery, bulk deletion and credential collection. More than 150 destructive or credential-collection operations ran over 35 minutes, hitting storage accounts, a Key Vault, a Function App and an App Service plan; SQL deletions failed on an unsupported API version and some deletions were stopped by resource locks. Microsoft saw no ransom note and did not confirm data exfiltration. The actor is tracked as Storm-3168 and is associated with JADEPUFFER, which Sysdig reported in July 2026 as the first documented agentic ransomware operation.

timeline.text: Early June: the first service principal enumerates VMs, subscriptions and resources for about 15.5 hours; the second follows about 90 minutes later and later enumerates App Service configuration stores. (Microsoft gives the month only; the 1st is a placeholder.)
Sysdig discovers JADEPUFFER (as reported by Microsoft). (Microsoft gives the month only; the 1st is a placeholder.)
Microsoft Security Research publishes the analysis.

stories.rootCause: Initial access is unconfirmed. Microsoft found a client ID, secret and tenant ID posted in plaintext in a public GitHub issue by an employee and still visible in the edit history, but could not confirm that credential was used. The service principals held broad Azure RBAC roles (Contributor, Storage Account Contributor, SQL DB Contributor), which made the deletions possible.
attacker: Used existing Azure RBAC assignments of the two service principals; five unique tokens for the destructive principal, two active in the same 70-second window, assessed as automated.
User agent python-requests/2.34.2 and shared infrastructure for both principals.
Tried to delete Azure Site Recovery and Azure Backup protection locks (failed), then listed storage account keys 30+ times after the destruction.
iocs: 45.131.66[.]106 (App Service probing and malicious ARM requests)

remediation.text: Treat publicly exposed credentials as compromised even after the source is edited: rotate immediately and review historical use.
Apply least privilege to service principals through Azure RBAC and prefer mechanisms that reduce long-lived credentials.
Use resource locks and deletion protection, restrict access to backup and recovery resources and monitor attempts to change their protection.
Enable the Defender for Cloud plans for Resource Manager, Storage, Key Vault, App Service and Databases.

apps.did: One was used for about 15.5 hours of reconnaissance; the second carried out discovery, destruction and credential theft across two subscriptions.
apps.action: Rotate or revoke the exposed credentials and review their historical use; Microsoft gives no disable-or-delete guidance.

stories.title: Beyond source code: a self-service password reset on one account led to Azure DevOps pipelines and Kubernetes credentials
stories.summary: Microsoft's Detection and Response Team described an intrusion that began with a single user account taken over through self-service password reset (SSPR). The attacker registered their own authentication methods, then used legitimate admin tools and scripts to enumerate Azure DevOps repositories, projects and pipelines. A malicious pipeline harvested Kubernetes credentials (kubeconfig files); pipeline scripts were then changed to install the Atera remote management agent and the Chisel tunnelling tool. The page attributes the activity to Storm-3068 and gives no attack dates and no IOC values. The case shows how an identity weakness spreads when development platforms, pipelines and cloud infrastructure are tightly connected.

timeline.text: Microsoft publishes the incident-response write-up; the page gives no dates for the intrusion itself.

stories.rootCause: Initial access was abuse of self-service password reset on a user account, followed by registration of attacker-controlled authentication methods. The impact grew because the account's permissions reached Azure DevOps pipelines authorised for more than 50 resources. The page does not state a formal root cause.
attacker: Took over a user account through self-service password reset and registered their own authentication methods.
Enumerated Azure DevOps repositories, projects, pipelines and deployment environments with legitimate tools and scripts.
Created a pipeline that deployed a kube agent and collected kubeconfig files at scale.
Modified pipeline scripts to install the Atera agent and download the Chisel tunnelling utility; Chisel opened a reverse tunnel to an external IP address (value not published).
Committed seven stolen kubeconfig files to a repository.

remediation.text: Monitor password reset activity for unusual patterns, such as repeated attempts or activity across multiple users.
Limit privileged accounts' exposure to self-service password reset and require phishing-resistant MFA.
Require approvals for code changes, enforce branch protection and restrict direct commits to critical branches.
Control who can create, modify or run build and deployment pipelines; apply least privilege across identities, development platforms and cloud resources.
Review recently registered authentication methods on accounts that completed a password reset, and review Azure DevOps audit logs for new or changed pipelines.

stories.title: Sideloaded AppX package abuses Microsoft-signed web hosts to capture OAuth tokens (Huntress research)
stories.summary: Huntress researcher Andrew Schwartz showed that a sideloaded AppX package can use Microsoft-signed AppX web hosts such as WWAHost.exe to show a genuine Microsoft sign-in, complete MFA and hand the authorization code to attacker JavaScript, which exchanges it for access and refresh tokens. It is post-compromise: it needs code execution in the user's session and Developer Mode or an enterprise sideloading policy. It was proven end to end on Windows 11 24H2 against a test tenant with MFA. Huntress names no threat actor and discloses no attacker infrastructure, so this is a technique, not an observed campaign. The Entra sign-in looks like a normal Office sign-in with no risk flags.

timeline.text: Huntress publishes the research; the page gives no date for the testing itself.

stories.rootCause: A design issue in the shared WinRT activation layer: a sideloaded package with WindowsRuntimeAccess="all" in ContentUriRules gives remote JavaScript the WinRT surface, with no caller validation, and the legacy WebAuthenticationBroker is reachable from inside the host. Developer Mode or the AllowAllTrustedApps policy is the gating condition.
attacker: Registers a package with Add-AppxPackage -Register as a standard user; the manifest points ContentUriRules at an attacker server.
Calls WebAuthenticationBroker.authenticateAsync() with Microsoft Office's first-party client ID and the urn:ietf:wg:oauth:2.0:oob redirect URI.
The user sees a real Microsoft login with no address bar and completes MFA.
Receives the authorization code through the broker callback, exchanges it and exfiltrates the access and refresh tokens.
iocs: User agent MSAppHost/3.0 (Edge/18) reaching non-Microsoft destinations (broker leg: MSAuthHost/1.0)
Add-AppxPackage -Register from paths outside C:\Program Files\WindowsApps

remediation.text: Deploy the Sigma proxy rule on user agent MSAppHost/3.0 with a Microsoft domain allow-list tuned to your environment.
Audit Developer Mode across the fleet and disable 'Allow all trusted apps to install' by GPO.
Require compliant or managed devices for token issuance with Conditional Access and pair with Token Protection where available.
Shorten refresh-token lifetimes and enable Continuous Access Evaluation.

links.text: OAuth Token Theft Through Microsoft's Front Door

stories.title: Storm-0940 and the ARTEX AI framework: Microsoft ties the ConnectWise Cloud Backup compromise to a China-aligned actor
stories.summary: On 21 October Microsoft Threat Intelligence published its analysis of a large, AI-automated campaign by Storm-0940, which it describes as a China-state aligned actor active since 2021, using the open-source ARTEX penetration-testing framework. Microsoft says it assesses that Storm-0940 was responsible for the ConnectWise supply-chain compromise of the multi-tenant Cloud Backup application, and that the actor reached privileged cloud access in some cases less than three hours after first targeting. After taking control of ConnectWise application identities, the actor signed in to more than 2,250 downstream tenants through applications those customers had already trusted, and in some tenants moved on to Graph reconnaissance, credential additions to applications and privileged role changes, including one application that gave itself Global Administrator. Microsoft states this was not caused by a vulnerability in or compromise of Microsoft systems, and that a sign-in does not by itself prove data was accessed. The page does not say how the ConnectWise identities were first compromised.

timeline.text: Password-spray campaign starts from 144.172.64[.]99 against 327 accounts in eight organizations (10-14 Oct); about 151,000 failed logons, peak 2,900 failures per minute on 11 Oct.
Public reports of the ConnectWise compromise appear, citing IOCs in the same network range.
ConnectWise publishes an initial advisory, later expanded; one of its IPs matches 144.172.64[.]99.
Microsoft publishes the attribution and the hunting and detection guidance.

stories.rootCause: Microsoft names no software vulnerability. The contributing factors it lists are compromised multi-tenant application identities holding high privileges, the trust and consent customers had already granted to those applications, password spraying against Microsoft 365 accounts, and machine-speed automation. It does not describe how the ConnectWise identities were initially compromised.
attacker: Used ARTEX, a multi-agent LLM framework that can run autonomous tests from reconnaissance to data exfiltration, to speed up targeting.
Ran a cross-tenant password spray against Microsoft 365 and Exchange Online (10-14 Oct).
Took control of identities of several ConnectWise cloud applications and used them to authenticate to customer tenants without interactive user sign-in (about 2,900 attempts per minute).

In some tenants: Graph and directory reconnaissance, application credential changes for persistence, changes to identities, groups and privileged roles; one application self-assigned Global Administrator (T1098.003).
Microsoft notes that backdoor credentials added to applications can survive remediation of the compromised application.
iocs: IP 144.172.64[.]99 (password spray; matches a ConnectWise advisory IP)
User agents Python-urllib/3.12, python-requests/2.31.0, python-requests/2.34.2, curl/7.88.1, azure-toolkit/1.0
ConnectWise application IDs 506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae (Cloud Backup), 24205314-2b89-4e07-a2a4-579e898a5640 (MS Teams), 0de14c77-b9b0-4137-9360-34878a929827 (MS Graph)

remediation.text: Keep the affected ConnectWise application connections disabled until ConnectWise gives formal restoration instructions; do not delete the enterprise applications first, preserve configuration and evidence.
Inventory the application IDs above and record the local service principal object IDs in each tenant; search by application ID, not display name.

Preserve Entra sign-in and audit logs, Purview Audit records and Graph telemetry; review service-principal sign-ins from at least 15 Oct, extended to 1 Oct, successes and failures separately and not only the published IPs.

Review Entra audit records for credential additions, new apps, service principals or owners, app-role assignments, consent grants, privileged role assignments and changes to authentication methods or Conditional Access; review mailbox forwarding, inbox and transport rules and delegate permissions.
After preserving evidence, have an authorized responder remove confirmed unauthorized credentials, grants, owners, assignments and identities, revoke unneeded permissions and rotate credentials.
Apply least privilege to multi-tenant application permissions and consent grants; alert on credential additions, privileged role assignment and anomalous app-only activity.
An empty hunting result is not proof of no access: Microsoft says so explicitly, so check the audit trail as well.

stories.title: PHP2Shell: two critical PHP remote code execution flaws (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619)
stories.summary: On 21 October 2026 the PHP project shipped emergency fixes for two critical flaws nicknamed PHP2Shell: CVE-2026-109618 (out-of-memory corruption) and CVE-2026-109619 (stale global state), both rated CVSS 4.0 9.2 by the sources. Every PHP installation serving web requests is affected, including PHP-FPM, mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed. A working exploit exists that needs a single unauthenticated request, and Amazon recorded an exploitation attempt on 17 October, four days before disclosure. Sources disagree on in-the-wild exploitation after disclosure, so treat it as exploited. Palo Alto Networks says all PAN-OS and Panorama versions are affected with no fix yet. This is not a Microsoft product flaw; it matters to the SOC for web servers, App Service/IIS-PHP hosts and appliances in the estate.

timeline.text: Amazon MadPot honeypot records a PHP2Shell exploitation attempt.
PHP releases fixes in 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27, 8.5.12 and source backports for 7.4, 8.0, 8.1; details leaked before the planned embargo.
Searchlight Cyber releases an open-source scanner; Palo Alto Networks confirms all PAN-OS and Panorama versions affected, no fix yet.

stories.rootCause: Memory-safety flaws in the PHP engine: out-of-memory handling can interrupt PHP while request data is only partly initialised (CVE-2026-109618), and request-owned state can outlive freed memory (CVE-2026-109619).
attacker: Unauthenticated remote code execution with a single request (per Help Net Security).
A pre-disclosure attempt from an IP tied to a commercial anonymisation service was seen by Amazon; how the exploit details were obtained is unknown.

remediation.text: Update PHP to 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27 or 8.5.12, or install the distribution/LTS vendor backport; take offline any system that cannot be fixed immediately (UK NCSC).
Cloudflare WAF rules for known vectors are a partial control only, not a substitute for patching.
Inventory PHP hosts (web servers, App Service/containers, appliances) and PHP versions; scan with the Searchlight Cyber php2shell-scanner.
Hunt web-server and process telemetry on PHP hosts for unexpected child processes of php-fpm/apache/php-cgi and new files in web roots since 17 October.

stories.title: LiteLLM 1.107.0 supply chain compromise: credential theft through Python startup hooks
stories.summary: A malicious LiteLLM 1.107.0 was published to PyPI on 21 October 2026 and also shipped in official container images. It abused Python startup hooks (a .pth file and sitecustomize.py placed outside the litellm directory), so the payload ran when the Python interpreter started, even if LiteLLM was never imported. The collector gathers developer, cloud, CI/CD and AI-tool credentials, encrypts them and posts them to www[.]litellm[.]dev. Per the LiteLLM maintainers, stolen developer GitHub credentials were used to alter the release workflow; Microsoft did not determine how the attacker first got upstream access. Microsoft published detections on 22 October and its analysis on 23 October. Removing the package or a release tag is not sufficient recovery.

timeline.text: LiteLLM 1.107.0 published to PyPI and distributed through official container images.
Microsoft Defender detections and vulnerability management entry TVM-2026-0003 available.
Microsoft publishes its analysis, including hashes, detections and hunting queries.

stories.rootCause: Per LiteLLM maintainers (as relayed by Microsoft): stolen developer GitHub credentials were used to alter the release workflow so it pointed at the lookalike repository Berri-AI/litellm instead of BerriAI/litellm, and a credential from another developer account satisfied a production approval step. How the attacker first obtained upstream access is not determined.
attacker: Used Python startup hooks (MITRE T1546.018): cook.pth imports cook.py, which decodes an embedded collector (PRIVCOLLECT) and runs it in a daemon thread; sitecustomize.py adds a Unix path with a remote code loader.

Targeted developer and AI tool configs, git and package-manager credentials, dotenv and key files, AWS/Azure CLI/GCP/Kubernetes/Docker credentials, browser data, shell histories and LiteLLM proxy database fields.
Encrypted the data (AES-256-CBC, key wrapped with an embedded RSA-4096 key) and sent it by HTTP POST to /healthcheck; staging directories begin with .pc_e_.
Unix loader reads a GitHub-hosted domain.txt as a pointer to an attacker server and executes the /codepy response; when examined domain.txt was empty and no second stage was confirmed.
iocs: Further wheel and variant hashes are listed in the Microsoft article

remediation.text: Find every copy: installed environments, uv and pip caches, internal mirrors, lock files, build outputs and container images; compare against the published hashes and scope mutable container tags.
Investigate from a known-clean system; do not run python or pip inside a suspect environment, because site processing can trigger the payload.
Rebuild from verified artifacts and confirm cook.pth, cook.py and sitecustomize.py are gone from the library path; deleting only the litellm directory is insufficient.

Rotate credentials from a clean machine (model-provider keys, cloud and CI/CD secrets, source-control and registry tokens, SSH/GPG keys, AI coding-tool tokens, DATABASE_URL on proxy hosts) and revoke sessions, not only passwords.
Hash-pin lock files, verify provenance, use image digests and restrict outbound access from build and AI workloads.
Hunt in Defender XDR for connections to www.litellm.dev and the listed file hashes; review Entra sign-ins and cloud activity for identities whose secrets lived on affected hosts.

kql.title: Connections to the collector domain (own minimal query)
kql.query:
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "litellm.dev"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP

stories.title: Zimbra SNMP command injection (CVE-2026-73570): one crafted SMTP request gives a shell on internet-facing mail servers
stories.summary: Microsoft Threat Intelligence describes exploitation of CVE-2026-73570 in Zimbra Collaboration Suite servers that have the optional zimbra-snmp package installed and SNMP notifications enabled. A crafted SMTP request reaches SNMP notification processing, and when health monitoring fires, the swatchdog component passes the attacker's value into a snmptrap shell call, so commands run as the zimbra service account. Attackers deployed JSP webshells on every mailbox node, escalated to root through a writable log directory and a PAM hook, persisted with a fake zimlog.service unit, and pulled zimbraPreAuthKey, zimbraAuthTokenKey and two-factor secrets from LDAP. On one server mailbox backups were archived and AzCopy was run against an Azure Blob SAS URL; Microsoft does not confirm the transfer completed. Zimbra 10.1.20 (20 July 2026) fixes it.

timeline.text: Zimbra 10.1.20 released with the remediation.
Scanning and probing of the injection point begins (to 7 August), with out-of-band DNS, HTTP and ICMP callbacks and the User-Agent ZB73570.
Public disclosure of CVE-2026-73570.
Microsoft Threat Intelligence publishes the attack chain, detections, hunting queries and IOCs.

stories.rootCause: Insufficient sanitisation of input that reaches the snmptrap shell invocation built by swatchdog in the optional zimbra-snmp package; commands run with the privileges of the zimbra service account.
attacker: Probed with curl, wget, ping, nslookup and id callbacks (User-Agent ZB73570).
Wrote JSP webshells into Jetty and mailboxd paths on every mailbox node, copied with rsync over the zimbra SSH identity.
Escalated to root by symlinking zmmailboxd.out to /etc/pam.d/sudo, adding a pam_exec hook and a NOPASSWD sudoers entry for zimbra.
Persisted with a timestomped zimlog.service systemd unit, cron, OpenRC, shell startup files, SSH keys and local accounts.
Read service credentials with zmlocalconfig -s and LDAP secrets (zimbraPreAuthKey, zimbraAuthTokenKey, zimbraTwoFactorAuthSecret).
Staged /opt/zimbra/final.tar.gz and invoked AzCopy with an Azure Blob SAS URL.

remediation.text: Upgrade every Zimbra Collaboration Suite instance to 10.1.20 or later.
If patching must wait: uninstall zimbra-snmp, disable SNMP notifications and restrict SNMP and SMTP to trusted hosts.
Treat a reverse-shell alert on an internet-facing mail server as a priority incident.
Check Zimbra application and servlet work directories on every mailbox node for unexpected JSP files and recent permission changes; review systemd units, PAM files and sudoers.
Rotate every domain zimbraPreAuthKey, and treat zimbraAuthTokenKey and stored two-factor secrets as exposed on a compromised server.
Search beyond the 30 days of advanced hunting data in Sentinel or archived logs.
Onboard Linux mail servers to Defender for Endpoint and confine the service account with namespace, seccomp or AppArmor controls.
Search Azure Storage logs for writes from the mail servers' public IPs, and alert when AzCopy runs on a mail server.

stories.title: Star Blizzard RedFlick: one click from a phishing archive to the CosmicPulse backdoor via scheduled tasks
stories.summary: Microsoft Threat Intelligence tracks RedFlick, a delivery technique used by the Russian state actor Star Blizzard from January to August 2026 against Ukrainian institutions, NGOs, think tanks, governments and financial institutions; Microsoft counts over 100 affected organizations, mostly in the US and UK. A first email without an attachment invites a reply; the follow-up carries a password-protected RAR or ZIP with the password shown as an image. Inside, an LNK disguised as a PDF runs SSH.exe with PermitLocalCommand or curl and PowerShell to fetch an MSI, which creates scheduled tasks that use control.exe to load the CosmicPulse downloader as a Control Panel applet. The post describes no OAuth, device-code or token abuse.

timeline.text: January campaign: VHDX with an LNK and BAT script that runs SSH.exe to fetch a remote MSI (activity observed from January).
From March, senders use accounts on compromised CPanel and WordPress sites instead of free mail services.
April: the MSI creates three scheduled tasks, including WebDAV loading through Control_RunDLL.
July: payload hidden in a downloaded PDF after the marker cAB, extracted by PowerShell.
August: steganography and a unique ZIP per target.
Microsoft Threat Intelligence publishes the analysis, detections, hunting queries and IOCs.

stories.rootCause: Social engineering: a reply-based phishing conversation followed by a password-protected archive that mail scanning cannot open, and a single user click on an LNK disguised as a PDF.
attacker: Sent tens to hundreds of lure emails per campaign impersonating Ukrainian authorities or conference invitations, some made to look internal.
Delivered password-protected RAR/ZIP archives with the password as an image.
Ran SSH.exe with PermitLocalCommand=yes and LocalCommand=cmd.exe, or conhost and curl, to fetch an MSI.

Created scheduled tasks (Internet Quality Test Connection, Network Configuration Manager, System Health Monitor) that use control.exe to load the CosmicPulse downloader (NOROBOT / BAITSWITCH) as a CPL.
Stored an encrypted AES key under HKCU\Software\Classes\.mollis and fetched a Python 3.8 bootstrapper and the CosmicPulse backdoor (YESROBOT).
iocs: secure-dns-hub[.]com (CosmicPulse DLL host, July to current)
Scheduled task names Internet Quality Test Connection, Network Configuration Manager, System Health Monitor

remediation.text: Use phishing-resistant authentication and Conditional Access policies.
Turn on Defender for Office 365 Safe Links, Safe Attachments and zero-hour auto purge.
Run EDR in block mode with cloud-delivered and real-time protection and network protection; enable ASR rules that block untrusted executables and obfuscated scripts.
Restrict outbound SSH from networks that do not need it.
Hunt for conhost.exe launching curl and ssh.exe with PermitLocalCommand=yes, and for the three scheduled task names; block the listed domains and IPs.
Alert on control.exe loading a CPL from a WebDAV UNC path or a user-writable folder, and quarantine password-protected archives from external senders for review.

kql.title: Scheduled tasks created by msiexec or control.exe in the last 30 days
kql.query:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/create"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Internet Quality Test Connection", "Network Configuration Manager", "System Health Monitor")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName

kqlPublished.title: Conhost.exe invokes curl
kqlPublished.query:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName == "conhost.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "curl"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, DeviceId, ProcessId, ProcessUniqueId, InitiatingProcessUniqueId

kqlPublished.title: Invoke SSH to launch local command line
kqlPublished.query:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "ssh.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "PermitLocalCommand=yes"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "LocalCommand=cmd.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, DeviceId, ProcessId, InitiatingProcessId, ReportId

stories.title: Token-replay spray against Microsoft 365: AiTM-stolen tokens replayed from 1337 Services hosting, 97 accounts at 79 organizations, attacker MFA and rogue Entra devices for persistence
stories.summary: Huntress (22 October 2026) describes a campaign observed from 14 July to 22 September 2026 in which tokens captured through adversary-in-the-middle phishing were replayed at scale from attacker-controlled hosts, an approach it calls token spraying. It counts more than 200,000 failed sign-ins from 193.26.115.0/24 (AS210558, 1337 Services GmbH), 497 successful Microsoft 365 sign-ins, 97 compromised accounts in 79 organizations and 48 rogue Entra devices. In at least 19 organizations the attacker removed existing MFA methods and registered its own authenticator within three hours of the first sign-in, then hid mail about payroll, deposits and bonuses with short-named inbox rules. The replayed sessions used Microsoft first-party clients (Microsoft Office, Microsoft Authentication Broker, OfficeHome) with node or bare Mozilla/5.0 user agents.

timeline.text: First activity in the campaign window Huntress measured.
In one case an authenticator named 'iPhone 13' was activated less than 51 minutes after the session was hijacked.
Last activity in the measured window.
Huntress publishes the analysis.
The Hacker News reports it.

stories.rootCause: Credentials and MFA were relayed through adversary-in-the-middle phishing pages, and the resulting tokens were replayed from hosting infrastructure; Conditional Access did not require MFA or block for every client app type, and device-code flow was not restricted.
attacker: Replayed stolen tokens from 193.26.115.0/24 and other 1337 Services addresses within minutes, across many organizations at once.
Used the Microsoft Office and Microsoft Authentication Broker clients with a node or bare Mozilla/5.0 user agent (Build A), and OfficeHome with a normal Chrome/Edge user agent (Build B).
Registered its own authenticator app after removing existing MFA methods in at least 19 organizations.
Joined 48 rogue devices to Entra ID, named DESKTOP- followed by eight hex characters.
Created inbox rules with names such as '.', 'sss', 'ss', 'iT', ',.', 's' and 'd' that deleted or moved payroll, deposit and bonus mail to RSS Feeds, RSS Subscriptions or Conversation History.
In one mailbox marked all mail read, deleted it and sent spam to hundreds of external recipients until Entra ID Protection flagged the user as high risk.
iocs: Rogue device names: DESKTOP-54521F46, DESKTOP-BAF88EF4, DESKTOP-CA85907C (pattern DESKTOP- + 8 hex)

apps.name: Microsoft Office
apps.did: Client application of the replayed sign-ins (Build A).
apps.action: Do not disable; hunt for its sign-ins from hosting IPs with a node or bare Mozilla/5.0 user agent

apps.name: Microsoft Authentication Broker
apps.did: Client application of replayed sign-ins (Build A), including Device Registration Service access used to join rogue devices.
apps.action: Do not disable; hunt for its sign-ins to Device Registration Service from hosting IPs

apps.name: OfficeHome
apps.did: Client application of replayed sign-ins (Build B) with a normal browser user agent.
apps.action: Do not disable; correlate with sign-ins from the listed ranges

stories.appsNote: Huntress names no attacker-created OAuth application; the IDs above are Microsoft's own clients the replay used. Resource IDs it lists (Microsoft Graph, Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, Device Registration Service 01cb2876-7ebd-4aa4-9cc9-d28bd4d359a9) are the targets, not attacker apps.

remediation.text: Revoke the user's sessions and reset the password; a reset alone leaves attacker devices, MFA methods and a valid token in place.
Audit registered MFA methods for ones cleared and re-registered within minutes and remove any unrecognized authenticator.
Audit Entra devices named DESKTOP-, Device- or Work Pc plus eight hex characters, especially ones registered from hosting IPs; confirm before deleting.
Review inbox rules with punctuation-only or very short names, or that move mail to RSS or Conversation History folders or match payroll and banking terms.
Treat AADSTS53003 blocks as evidence of a valid stolen credential, not a successful defense.
Restrict device-code flow with a Conditional Access authentication-flows policy and require MFA or block for all users, all cloud apps and all client app types.

Hunt sign-in logs for the Microsoft Office or Authentication Broker client from AS210558 or 193.26.115.0/24 with a node or bare Mozilla/5.0 user agent, and alert on MFA method registration within three hours of a sign-in from a hosting ASN.
Block standard users from consenting to applications and review newly consented enterprise applications for the affected users.

stories.title: Fake IT support over Teams external chat: mail bombing, throwaway onmicrosoft.com tenants and RMM tools lead to GoGRPC, Python implants and Chaos ransomware
stories.summary: Arctic Wolf Labs (26 October 2026) describes a recurring pattern across hundreds of cases: the victim's inbox is flooded with subscription mail, then an 'IT support' account from a throwaway tenant (30-40% on onmicrosoft.com fallback domains) opens a Teams external chat and talks the user into a remote session through Quick Assist, AnyDesk, ScreenConnect, TeamViewer or another RMM tool. Instead of pasting links, the attacker has the user run PowerShell that pulls an MSI from Azure Blob Storage, which unpacks a Python implant; a second MSI queries Active Directory over LDAP for every computer and user and sends the result out. Follow-on activity includes the GoGRPC backdoor, Level RMM for redundancy, lateral movement to domain controllers, exfiltration and ransomware; the activity aligns with STAC4749, linked by Sophos to Chaos ransomware.

timeline.text: Arctic Wolf Labs publishes the analysis with tenant domains and .top infrastructure.
The Hacker News reports it.

stories.rootCause: Teams external access open to any tenant (including trial tenants), users able to accept remote-control sessions from an unsolicited contact, and RMM tools that could be installed or run without approval.
attacker: Mail-bombed the target with newsletter and subscription confirmations.
Opened Teams external chats from throwaway tenants with IT-themed display names (Help Desk, IT Support, IT Service Desk - Liam, HelpDesk Supervisor).
Gained hands-on-keyboard access through Quick Assist, AnyDesk, ScreenConnect, TeamViewer, Atera, Zoho Assist, NetSupport or LogMeIn.
Had the user run PowerShell that downloaded an MSI from Azure Blob Storage, dropping a Python implant (ss.py, cleaner.ps1 under AppData\Local\PowershellCleaner\scripts).
Enumerated all Active Directory users and computers over LDAP and exfiltrated the results; deployed GoGRPC and Level RMM; moved to domain controllers and deployed ransomware.
iocs: update-software[.]top, infoupdate-it[.]top, soft-program[.]top, getsysmonitor[.]top, expertassist[.]top, sec-check-it[.]top, techrelay[.]top, ms-system-check[.]top, it-assistant[.]top, get-help[.]top

remediation.text: Switch Teams external access from allow-all to an allow-list of specific external domains.
Block federation with trial tenants: Set-CsTenantFederationConfiguration -ExternalAccessWithTrialTenants "Blocked".
Block chat with unmanaged Teams accounts and stop them from starting conversations with your users.
Enable 'Allow my security team to manage blocked domains' and add the listed tenant domains to the Defender Tenant Allow/Block List.
Restrict Quick Assist to authorized IT roles and block or uninstall unsanctioned RMM tools through Defender for Endpoint or application control.
Require out-of-band verification for every remote-access request and tell staff how real IT contacts them.

Search CloudAppEvents for ChatCreated with a participant from the listed onmicrosoft.com tenants and, on hits, look on that user's device for an RMM process start followed by PowerShell, msiexec and LDAP queries.

stories.title: YAM Store (Storm-3119) and the Storm-2990 phishing kits: a marketplace of hijacked Microsoft 365 tenants and phishing-as-a-service, disrupted by Microsoft DCU
stories.summary: Microsoft Threat Intelligence and the Digital Crimes Unit (14 October 2026) describe YAM Store, a Chinese-language initial-access marketplace tracked as Storm-3119 that sells compromised or fraudulently created Microsoft and Google environments, credentials and infrastructure, and Storm-2990, the developers of the CoGUI, Haozi and Iron Man System phishing kits sold through it. Microsoft says the kits' operators facilitated over one billion phishing emails and SMS messages to more than 75,000 organizations since January 2026. YAM Store discovers Microsoft 365 tenants, takes them over with compromised client secrets in an app-only flow, and abuses a compromised Global Administrator to provision the PnP Management Shell service principal with broad Graph and SharePoint permissions for bulk hosting. Microsoft DCU, with law enforcement and partners, disrupted the ecosystem's primary developers and infrastructure.

timeline.text: From January 2026 the kits' operators facilitate over one billion phishing emails and SMS messages to more than 75,000 organizations (Microsoft's figure; start month only).
Iron Man System starts being advertised through YAM Store (Microsoft gives the month only).
Microsoft publishes the analysis; the Digital Crimes Unit facilitated disruption of the primary developers and infrastructure with law enforcement and partners.

stories.rootCause: Compromised client secrets of applications in victim tenants (used in an application-only authentication flow) and compromised Global Administrator accounts, plus fraudulently created tenants backed by fake organizations.
attacker: Discovered Microsoft 365 tenants and their licensing with automated Flask-based tooling run over Tor.
Used compromised client secrets in an app-only flow to reset passwords, assign education licences and grant privileged attributes silently.

Signed in as a compromised Global Administrator, provisioned the PnP Management Shell service principal and granted it broad Graph permissions (including AppCatalog.ReadWrite.All) and full SharePoint API control.
Abused SharePoint and OneDrive for bulk hosting and ran a custom DNS platform for phishing domains and certificates behind Cloudflare.
Sold phishing kits with geofencing, fake CAPTCHA gates, Telegram-bot exfiltration and WebSocket live victim interaction; downstream buyers ran credential phishing and device-code phishing.

apps.name: PnP Management Shell
apps.did: Provisioned by the attacker from a compromised Global Administrator account and granted broad Graph permissions (including AppCatalog.ReadWrite.All) and full SharePoint API control to abuse SharePoint and OneDrive storage.
apps.action: Not stated by Microsoft; review any service principal for it created without a change record (our proposal)

stories.appsNote: Microsoft names the PnP Management Shell service principal but prints no application ID; none is given here.

remediation.text: Use phishing-resistant MFA through Conditional Access for privileged accounts and lock down Global Administrator roles.
Restrict MFA and passkey registration to trusted locations and devices.
Configure Safe Links to apply to internal recipients and review the recommended Exchange Online Protection and Defender for Office 365 settings.
Enable network protection.
List service principals created in the last 90 days with SharePoint or AppCatalog permissions, starting with PnP Management Shell, and confirm each has an owner and a change record.
Rotate client secrets on applications that hold directory-write permissions and remove secrets nobody can account for.

stories.title: Masqueraded MSP360 RMM installer (v2.5.0.67) used to plant ConnectWise ScreenConnect through phishing lures
stories.summary: Microsoft Defender Experts observed phishing campaigns in July 2026, across multiple industries, that delivered a signed but masqueraded MSP360 RMM installer (v2.5.0.67) behind lures such as e-card and RSVP invitations, Zoom and Adobe Reader installers, document signing, job offers and delivery notices. Once a user ran it and approved UAC, the agent installed as two Windows services, opened UDP 48678 inbound and launched PowerShell that downloaded and silently installed ConnectWise ScreenConnect as a second remote-access channel. The actor then used ScreenConnect's RunFile feature to drop tools named to look like Windows, Defender or Phone Link components for credential theft, collection and hiding the session. Microsoft saw no exploitation of ScreenConnect itself and does not attribute the activity; it says the installer's signing certificate has since been revoked.

timeline.text: Defender Experts observe the phishing campaigns distributing the masqueraded MSP360 v2.5.0.67 installer; a separate July activity uses FaronicsDeployAgent.exe the same way (Microsoft gives the month only).
Microsoft publishes the analysis with detections, hunting queries and indicators.

stories.rootCause: Users ran a signed remote-management installer delivered by phishing and approved its UAC prompt; legitimately obtained RMM software then gave the actor persistent, trusted remote access.
attacker: Hosted payloads on attacker domains, compromised sites, Amazon S3, Cloudflare R2, Dropbox, GitLab and Supabase.
Installed the MSP360 agent to C:\Program Files\RMM Agent\ as services RMM.Agent.exe and RMM.Agent.Launcher.exe, with Run keys and an inbound firewall rule on UDP 48678.
Ran PowerShell from RMM.Agent.exe to fetch ClientSetup.msi with Invoke-WebRequest and install ScreenConnect with msiexec /qn.
Used ScreenConnect RunFile to execute tools from Documents\ScreenConnect\Temp, including WebBrowserPassView.exe, DefenderControl.exe, WindowsSecurity_Password.exe and SCHider.exe.

remediation.text: Hunt for the MSP360 installer hash and for unapproved RMM installations; where found, reset the passwords of the accounts used to install the RMM services and investigate further if a system-level account was used.
Block unapproved IT management tools with Application Control for Windows or AppLocker publisher rules, and use the Defender for Endpoint block-certificate action for signed installers.
Enable cloud-delivered protection and the ASR rules 'Use advanced protection against ransomware' and 'Block process creations originating from PsExec and WMI commands'.
Enforce MFA on the RMM platforms you approve.
Isolate a device that runs RMM.Agent.exe or a ScreenConnect client you did not deploy, uninstall both and remove the UDP 48678 firewall rule before reconnecting it.
Alert on new services or Run keys for remote-access tools outside your approved RMM list, and on processes started from \ScreenConnect\Temp\.
